skyline.text: The state should be legible to us, says Amit Varma
Ajay Shah calls neat plantations ignorance dressed up as science
Newton’s gracious line was really a jab at Robert Hooke

footnote.text: So you think seeing is free. Actually, seeing is very hard.

brief.head: Pass the baton
brief.text: Change comes through a relay of ideas, Ajay Shah said. Short-termists cheer the last runner; you have to see everyone who handed the baton upstream. {115-C01}

brief.head: After the Wall fell
brief.text: Once the USSR collapsed, Ajay Shah said, many in democracies drifted towards technocratic social engineering. “Now that the USSR is gone, let’s be a little bit more like the USSR.” {115-C02}

brief.head: Delete by default
brief.text: When you pay a toll, the state learns where your car was. Ajay Shah wants such data deleted within seconds unless the people authorise keeping it. {115-C07}

brief.head: Safe in Norway
brief.text: Electronic payments are reasonably safe in Norway and a prison in North Korea, Ajay Shah said. How much a state may see should depend on its freedoms. {115-C15}

brief.head: A thousand Singapores
brief.text: India is a thousand Singapore-sized locales, Ajay Shah said, so one ruler instructing all of it is “a recipe for trouble”. {#locales}

thought.text: Deep down inside I know the unseen, I know the cost.
thought.who: Amit Varma, admitting that Chandigarh’s wide roads and clean air hide a price

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on James C Scott’s classic
lead.head: The state that can’t see the trees
body: Amit Varma opened with a rock band. Only thirty people bought the Velvet Underground’s albums, it was once said, and all thirty became musicians. James C Scott, he argued, is the Velvet Underground of ideas. {115-J12}
Mention Scott in public and people say “James who?”, Varma said. Yet he is “a dominant influence on many others who are dominant influences on the world at large”.
The episode was given over to Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*, the 1998 book that changed Ajay Shah’s life. Its subtitle asks why certain schemes to improve the human condition have failed.

Some of the smartest people in the world, Shah said, led such schemes. P C Mahalanobis was a great physicist and a great statistician. “And yet when it came to thinking about society, his stuff was phenomenally wrong.” {115-C03}
## Three tools
Shah set out the book as a toolkit of three ideas.

The first is state legibility. A person sees without effort; a state sees only when an official writes something on file, with all the discretion, bribery and secrecy that invites. So states force people to become easier to read, with consequences nobody intended.
The second is high modernism, “the belief that scientists and engineers have a superior claim upon knowledge about society”, imposed from the top by the coercive power of the state. {115-C08}
The third is metis: local, tacit knowledge gained by doing, which cannot be written into a manual and which changes if you move a hundred kilometres.
## A forest made countable

Scott’s central example is Prussian scientific forestry, which Shah said is just as much the story of British forestry in India. The forest is reduced to one aim, timber, and replanted as a monoculture in clean rows.
It is easy to count and easy to kill. One insect or one fungus can wipe it out, and the soil is degraded. “This is ignorance. It’s not science,” Shah said. {115-C10}
Things go worst, Scott argues, when four elements meet: a high-modernist philosophy, state power used to make society legible, an authoritarian state and a civil society too weak to push back.

Shah’s examples ran from Stalin’s collective farms to Brasília, Bombay’s Bandra Kurla Complex and India’s Green Revolution. Varma confessed that he was born in Chandigarh, a city designed by “one of the villains of high modernism”.
## Humility, not abolition
Scott does not want the state to wither away, Shah said. We need a monopoly of violence, law and order and monetary policy. The message is humility: make small moves that can be undone.
“The state has a lust for arbitrary power,” he said, just as firms lust for profit. So every new way for the state to see must come with commensurate checks and balances.
Varma turned the question around. “We don’t need to be legible to them,” he said. “The state needs to be legible to us.” {115-C06}

The toolkit, Shah said, is an engine for thinking about the world, well beyond governments. He set listeners a challenge: take any episode of the show and write a comment on how it links to *Seeing Like a State*.
Varma took it up at once with the show’s cycling episode. What is a formation of cyclists in slipstream, he asked, “if not high modernism”?

second.label: Soviet collectivisation
second.head: Seeds sown in 1932
second.deck: Ajay Shah traces a 1991 vote and a Soviet collapse to Stalin’s farms
body: Stalin could be very pragmatic in some respects, Ajay Shah said. On collectivisation he was “a bloody minded ideologue”. When rich farmers resisted the state taking their land, he crushed them with extreme brutality.

In Ukraine, Stalin blocked off the food supply and the Soviets grabbed the grain. Somewhere between 4 and 10 per cent of Ukraine’s population died in a man-made famine. In 1991, Shah noted, 90 per cent of Ukraine voted to leave Russia. {115-S03}

The scheme cast a longer shadow. By the mid-80s, the Soviet economy rested on exporting crude oil and importing grain. {#crude} When the price of crude fell and the price of grain rose, Shah said, the USSR collapsed.

quote.text: The seeds of the 1991 referendum where 90 per cent of Ukraine voted to leave Russia was sowed in 1932.

second.caption: Stalin’s collectivisation

third.head: The number before the law
body: Ajay Shah was in the debates over Aadhaar. The first Aadhaar number was issued in 2009, he said, on the understanding that a privacy law was coming: Manmohan Singh’s government was going to give it. {115-S04}
Then came Scott. Shah read *Seeing Like a State* only in 2012. “James C. Scott was slapping me around in 2012,” he said.
“Now I’m older and wiser,” Shah said. First show him the privacy law, and a powerful one, matching “the dangers of a single number that can be traced to every person in the country”.
He added a pointed observation. Biometric ID systems, he said, only happen in poor, relatively authoritarian developing countries, and not in advanced democracies. “I wonder why.” {#biometric}
third.caption: Aadhaar and the privacy law

p2.title: Reading the state
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s guide to James C Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*, from legibility to metis, argued over with Amit Varma. {115-R01}

sections.label: The first idea
sections.head: A bureaucracy has no eyes
sections.caption: state legibility
body: Seeing comes effortlessly to a human being, Ajay Shah said. A state is different. “In a state, policy is a mapping from a state of nature to a state action”: an official must look, write something on file, and only then does policy kick in. {115-C04}
Every step is fraught: an official’s discretion, the pull of a promotion or a bribe, the sheer size of India, the shakedowns that follow when seeing has consequences, and secrecy.
People hide, too. States have a grisly record of taxation, conscription and enslavement, Shah said, so people are not interested in being seen.
## Flattening the fields
Shah’s proposed T-shirt slogan sums up what follows: “State legibility schemes have unintended consequences.” Amit Varma said it would come only in triple XL. {115-J03}

Land shows why. One person owns it, another has the right to grow the Kharif crop on it, and a third grazes cattle there when it lies fallow. In a Burkean sense, Shah said, such arrangements evolved for a reason.

A state that insists on one owner with all the rights is “a bull in a China shop”. Its logic is the Domesday Book’s: “if you have the land, I’ll tax you and I want clarity on who has the land.” {115-J15}
~ Varma would reverse the flow. The state exists to serve us, not rule us, he said, so it is the government that should be utterly transparent and accountable. {115-C06}

quote.text: It’s the technocratic illusion that I’ll build a thousand man force and they’ll walk around the country and they’ll see.

sections.label: The second idea
sections.head: Not the same as modern
sections.caption: high modernism
body: When Amit Varma first heard the phrase high modernism, he thought it meant “you wear shirt pant and you do drugs”. {115-J04}
Ajay Shah set him straight. Modernity is a good thing: secular, individualist, free of superstition, with people dealing with one another as full persons rather than as kith, kin and tribe.
High modernism is something else. Varma compared the pair to popularity and populism: “They’re almost opposite things.” {115-J05}

It is, Shah said, “the belief that scientists and engineers have a superior claim upon knowledge about society”, and that they should reshape it through top-down schemes backed by the coercion of the state. It stands for “one India, one X”. {115-C08}
## Why the schemes fail
Partly, the planners lack the information. Partly, people respond to incentives: they hate the king, Shah said, and “smirk and smile” while quietly undermining the grand scheme.
The high modernist treats the past as an impediment to be swept away. Shah’s alternative is Burkean humility: make small moves, decentralise, rely on local knowledge.
~ India, he warned, is in a second wave of it, fed by the internet, tech billionaires, software success and a great regression in political philosophy. {#secondwave}

quote.text: High modernism is this fantasy that there can be some centralised rule and they will tell the people what to do.

sections.label: The third idea
sections.head: Knowledge you can’t write down
sections.caption: metis
body: The third idea is a word from Greek, which James C Scott imported into English: metis.

Scott separates objective, universal knowledge, such as special relativity, from most knowledge about human society. That, Ajay Shah said, is metis: “deep experiential knowledge. It’s not knowledge in a book.” {115-C09}

You have to be there and do things to gain it. It is tacit: “once I acquire the knowledge, I can’t write it in a book and give it to you,” Shah said. And it is local, changing from one place to the next.
## The opposite of a manual

Metis is not a single manual tossed down from above for everyone to follow. It carries judgment, humility and respect for how the world works. That makes it the exact opposite of high modernism, which says: “We know this, we’ve read this book, we know how to do this. Now everybody fall in line.”

Shah carries the idea into business. He looks at the arrogance of a giant national bank trying to run the whole bank through one process, one manual, and becomes sceptical, because “UP is not Maharashtra”. {#bank}
~ Amit Varma heard the same note in Jane Jacobs, whose work, he said, embodied an organic appreciation for spontaneous order and for metis. {115-R15}

quote.text: It is very local knowledge. You move hundred kilometres the knowledge will change.

sections.label: The example
sections.head: The forest as a timber farm
sections.caption: Prussian scientific forestry
body: The example James C Scott uses in the book is Prussian scientific forestry. Ajay Shah said it is equally the story of British colonial forestry in India, and that it begins with an abuse of the word science. “Dude don’t pull the science card on me,” he said. {115-J06}
The forest is taken to exist for one purpose: timber. Foresters pick the tree that yields the most cubic metres a year and plant a monoculture in clean, orderly rows.
At the Forest Research Institute in Dehradun, Shah said, experiments planted trees one metre or two metres apart, waited fifty years and counted the wood. {#forestry}
## A web, not a farm

A real forest is many species, richly interconnected and resilient: an insect or a fungus kills a few things and the forest is fine. The plantation strips the soil of micronutrients, and one insect or one fungus can destroy it all. {115-C10}

An inspector can count exactly a thousand trees. Legibility has been imposed and the forest destroyed. Explaining a joke, Shah said, is like dissecting a frog: “You can understand it, but it kills the frog.” {115-J14}
~ Amit Varma reached for Peter Wohlleben’s *The Hidden Life of Trees*, which made him realise that you cannot just plant forty trees together and call it an ecosystem. {115-R17}

quote.text: When people in the world of policy use the word science, you should start getting suspicious.

sections.label: The evidence
sections.head: From Daulatabad to Bandra
sections.caption: grand schemes that failed
body: Scott’s warning is a four-part test, Ajay Shah said: a high-modernist philosophy, state power used to render society legible, an authoritarian state, and a civil society too weak to push back. “When you get these four things together, you get absolutely bad outcomes.” {115-C11}

After Stalin’s farms, Shah turned to cities. There was “some bloke in Delhi” who thought of shifting the capital to Daulatabad; there was Brasília. “Humans don’t respond to a centrally planned push to make a city.”
Bimal Patel’s rule, which Shah endorsed, is that 40 per cent of the land should be streets and parks, and people should decide the rest. {#patel}
Bombay’s Bandra Kurla Complex, supposedly a financial centre, has towers but no room for coffee shops. {#bkc}
## The Green Revolution, revisited

Shah applied the same lens to the Green Revolution, which India remembers as its escape from PL 480. It was a top-down scheme of MSP, fertiliser subsidies, free electricity for pumps and a few cultivars of rice and wheat.

The longer bill includes pesticides in the groundwater, regions of Punjab and Haryana filled with cancer, and a groundwater crisis. The Netherlands, the area of Haryana, exports $140 billion of food. {#netherlands}
~ And the diet suffered. “We filled up the bellies of the people of India with starch,” Shah said. {115-C13}

quote.text: A financial centre is people. It is conversations over coffee that is a financial centre.

sections.label: The lessons
sections.head: Feeling for the stones
sections.caption: humility and checks and balances
body: Ajay Shah admitted he fought the book page by page. “Look, I was stupid,” he said. Scott is not proposing that the state wither away. His message is humility.

We need a state, Shah said: a monopoly of violence, law and order, monetary policy. But coercive power should be used with the greatest care. Vijay Kelkar and Shah’s own book has a chapter titled after Deng Xiaoping’s “Cross the River by Feeling the Stones”. {115-J17}
Make small moves, things you can undo, Shah said. Scott has a footnote giving this as one of the many reasons he has for opposing the death penalty. {#deathpenalty}
## Match the system to the country
“The state spreads its hands in ceaseless striving for more arbitrary power,” Shah said, and that striving must be met with commensurate checks and balances. {115-C14}

His yardstick is the Freedom House ranking, from Norway at the top to North Korea at the bottom. Medical records held by the state are fine in the UK, he said, but not in India. “So certain systems should not be in certain countries.” {115-C15}

~ The same humility argues for decentralisation. India covers 3.3 million square kilometres; every function, Shah said, belongs at the lowest level of government that can do it. Solving mass transport in Bombay is Bombay expertise.

quote.text: Every function of government should be done at the lowest level of government at which it can possibly be done.

side.boxText: *Seeing Like a State* came out in 1998 and spans political philosophy, sociology, anthropology, urban policy and development studies. By then, Ajay Shah said, James C Scott was “a Renaissance thinker”, and field after field took to the book. {#renaissance}

contQuote.text: Many short-termist people see that last mile that one runner gets across the race and they say, Yay. But you have to see all the people that handed the baton upstream.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Shelves, sparrows, giants and a stage play: the tales that carried the argument

stories.start: The book was released in 1998, and I frankly missed it completely.
stories.end: I just sat for a couple of days and only read this book.
stories.caption: the book on his shelf
stories.kicker: How Ajay Shah came, at last, to James C Scott
stories.head: The book that waited eight years
body: *Seeing Like a State* came out in 1998, and Ajay Shah missed it completely. Brad DeLong had written about it on his blog, which was in Shah’s RSS feed, but he failed to catch it there. {115-R04}

Some years later, around 2004 as he recalls, after the UPA government came to power, Lant Pritchett moved to Delhi. He gave Shah the book, with Chester Barnard’s *The Functions of the Executive*, and said it would change the way he thought about the world. {115-R05}
“I’m extremely embarrassed to say to you, I did not read it for a long time,” Shah said. From 2004 to 2012, it sat on his shelf. {#sat}

He had comfort for listeners in the same position. “Gentle reader, don’t beat yourself up too much because there are all these great books sitting on your shelf,” he said. “Our books are our companions.” Their physical presence, he argued, shapes the day you finally pull one out. {115-S01}
When that day came, he was blown away. He had been, he said, “a callow fool” back then, and page after page felt like an assault on him.
He fought back, arguing with Scott as he read; the book, he said, was unputdownable. He blew away all his meetings and spent a couple of days doing nothing but reading the book.
~ Much later in the episode, he put it more vividly: page after page, Scott was slapping him in the face.
stories.why: An unread book on the shelf is not a failure, Shah suggested: it waits for its day. And the books that change you most may be the ones you argue with, page after page.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma praised him for changing his mind: most people, he said, get ossified once their view of the world seems to explain everything.

stories.start: in a previous episode we've actually discussed Mao's high modernism, where he said
stories.end: actually destroyed all the crops and millions of people starved to death.
stories.caption: Mao’s sparrows
stories.kicker: Amit Varma recalls a war on birds, and its sequel
stories.head: No sparrows, no harvest
body: Ajay Shah had just finished taking apart scientific forestry when Amit Varma, “a big fan of angiosperms”, recalled a story about Mao’s high modernism that the hosts had discussed in an earlier episode.
Mao, he said, decided that all sparrows should be put to death, because they were harming crops.
But sparrows ate locusts. “Locusts proliferated after sparrows were killed and actually destroyed all the crops and millions of people starved to death,” Varma said. {115-S05}

~ Shah had just described a forest as many species, richly interconnected in a web of life, all symbiotic upon each other. {115-C10} Mao pulled out one thread, and the web gave way. There are many such examples, Varma added, from all across the world and from India, sadly.
stories.why: A top-down scheme built on one simple theory can upset a web nobody fully sees. Locusts followed sparrows, famine followed locusts: the costs of high modernism can arrive far from where the order was given.

stories.start: So first of all the original quote, uh I stood I I saw further
stories.end: were built out of Hooke's work, and this was Newton's
stories.caption: Newton and Hooke
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the petty origin of a gracious line
stories.head: A chip on Newton’s shoulder
body: Amit Varma thought of a quote, we all stand on the shoulders of giants, and then of another: he couldn’t get anywhere because giants were standing on his shoulder.

Ajay Shah supplied the history. The original line, about seeing further than others by standing on the shoulders of giants, is Newton’s. “Newton was a truly mean and unpleasant person,” he said. {115-S02}
Newton had a lifelong rivalry with Robert Hooke, who was a hunchback, and who had implied that Newton’s ideas were built out of his own work. The famous line was Newton’s put-down.

~ So, Varma asked, how could Shah, a nice guy, be a great thinker? “They are orthogonal,” Shah replied, and offered a Unix fortune instead: “in computer science we stand on each other’s shoulders.” {115-J13}

quote.text: The great man Newton was not a nice person.

stories.start: So there is a great play called Tuglak by Girishkarnad.
stories.end: This shows that people contain multitudes. Great follies can be made by great men.
stories.caption: Tughlaq and Nehru
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s abandoned college play, and its hidden target
stories.head: A ruler in Nehru’s clothing
body: At eighteen or nineteen, Amit Varma and a college friend tried to stage Girish Karnad’s *Tughlaq* as a two-man play.
It never happened. “Inevitably one of us was Bengali and hint it wasn’t him,” Varma said. “And therefore the project went to hell and I procrastinated.” {115-J10}

Tughlaq, he explained, was a high modernist who shifted his capital and did things to the currency, and all of it failed. Karnad wrote the play in the mid-sixties, as disillusionment with Nehruvian socialism set in. So the play was about Nehru too. {115-S08}

~ Varma did not know if Tughlaq was a great man, but Nehru certainly was, as Ajay Shah has said. Shah is comfortable separating art and artist: Nehru, in his words, was a great artist whose art “was like pretty bad in some ways”. {115-J07}

quote.text: This shows that people contain multitudes. Great follies can be made by great men.

stories.postscript: Varma regretted that *Tughlaq* was his only fiction pick, and promised more fiction, art and cinema from the next episode.

quiz.q: Which band did Amit Varma compare James C Scott to, and why?
quiz.a: The Velvet Underground: only thirty bought its albums, and all became musicians.

quiz.q: Who gave Ajay Shah the book around 2004, and when did he finally read it?
quiz.a: Lant Pritchett, after moving to Delhi; Shah read it only in 2012.

quiz.q: What single purpose does scientific forestry assign to a forest, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: Timber: the most cubic metres a year, from one species in rows.

quiz.q: Which four things together, in Scott’s test, produce absolutely bad outcomes?
quiz.a: High modernism, state legibility, an authoritarian state and a weak civil society.

quiz.q: Which Greek word did Scott bring into English, and what does it mean?
quiz.a: Metis: deep, local, experiential knowledge that cannot be written down in a book.

quiz.q: Why does Ajay Shah now say India built Aadhaar in the wrong order?
quiz.a: The privacy law should have come first, before the first number in 2009.
